node.label: Canadian regional history
node.period_rationale: Provincial syntheses (Morton 1957, Ormsby 1958) and the limited-identities argument (1967, 1969) fall in period_1; Acadiensis (1971) and the regional syntheses of the 1970s–90s carry the field into period_2 and period_3. groups.json gives period_1/period_2.
node.date_label: Morton's Manitoba 1957 · Ormsby's British Columbia 1958 · Craig's Upper Canada 1963 · 'limited identities' 1967–69 · Acadiensis 1971 · Acheson 1972 · Forbes 1979 · Friesen 1984 · Barman 1991 · reassessments 2000 · coverage through 2000

date_span.basis: Selected milestones; provincial and local history is much older. Engagement in 2009–2026 PhDs is steady.

node.description: Histories of Canada's regions as places with their own economies, societies and identities rather than as peripheries of a central-Canadian story. Provincial syntheses such as Morton's Manitoba (1957) and Ormsby's British Columbia (1958) preceded the 'limited identities' argument: Cook (1967) suggested that Canadianism might be found in regional, ethnic and class identities, and Careless (1969) made the phrase a programme. In 1971 Buckner founded Acadiensis, complaining that historians remained 'obsessed with the great "national" themes'. Acheson (1972) traced Maritime industrial growth under the National Policy and its subordination to Montreal capital, and Forbes studied the Maritime Rights movement (1979). Friesen's The Canadian Prairies (1984), Barman's The West Beyond the West (1991), Conrad and Hiller's Atlantic Canada (2001) and Waiser's Saskatchewan (2005) offered regional syntheses, while Owram, Carter and Harris tied western and Pacific history to expansionist ideas, reserve policy and colonial geography. Ontario had provincial histories of its own (Craig 1963; Nelles 1974; McCalla 1993). Acadia became a growing Atlantic literature: Griffiths on Acadian history and identity (1992, 2005), Plank and Faragher on conquest and expulsion (2001, 2005), and Reid, Basque and colleagues on 1710 (2004). Francophone regional history worked at other scales: Painchaud on the Church and French Prairie settlement (a 1970s study, published posthumously in 1987), Landry and Lang's Histoire de l'Acadie (2001), and Quebec's intraprovincial regional histories, which Harvey contrasts with interprovincial regionalism. By 2000 McKay asked whether 'region' could hold the new histories of gender, ethnicity and community, and Buckner revisited limited identities.
node.scope_note: A research field for Canada's regions (the Prairie West, British Columbia, the Atlantic provinces including Acadia, and Ontario) and the limited-identities argument. Provincial syntheses, regional economic history, rural history and regional identity are distinct strands. Indigenous and settler-colonial histories of the West and British Columbia overlap strongly (Carter, Harris) and are primarily placed in native_newcomer, settler_colonialism and environment. Ontario has a strand of provincial syntheses and economic histories chosen by PhD citation counts; Acadia has its own Atlantic strand. The North and Newfoundland are small in the PhD corpus (about 18 and 9 titles) and get only this note. Quebec's regional history appears only as a contrast of scale. Roster inclusion does not imply that historians accepted "limited identities".

representative_people.name: W. L. Morton
representative_people.context: Historian of Manitoba and the West; his provincial synthesis (1957) precedes the limited-identities argument. In 1946 he asked on what premises the established national interpretations rested (abstract).

representative_people.name: Margaret A. Ormsby
representative_people.context: Author of the centennial history of British Columbia (1958), which Barman later called "an invaluable beginning point" (as reported in BC Studies). Reimer's history of BC historical writing ends in 1958, the province's centenary and the year of her book, and treats her with W. Kaye Lamb as a first generation of BC historians (contents; Favrholdt's review). President of the Canadian Historical Association in 1965–66, its second woman president after Hilda Neatby (1962–63) (CHA list).

representative_people.name: Ramsay Cook
representative_people.context: Suggested in 1967 that Canadianism might be found in "the regional, ethnic and class identities that we do have" (quoted by Buckner). Primary placement proposed in cdn_intellectual_cultural.

representative_people.name: J. M. S. Careless
representative_people.context: Made "limited identities of region, culture and class" a programme for Canadian history (1969, via Buckner's quotations); later synthesized regions, cities and identities before 1914 (1989).
representative_people.works: "'Limited Identities' in Canada" (1969); Frontier and Metropolis (1989)

representative_people.name: Phillip Buckner
representative_people.context: Founded Acadiensis (1971) against historians "obsessed with the great 'national' themes"; defended limited identities from an Atlantic perspective (1988) and revisited the concept (2000). Primary placement proposed in cdn_political_national.
representative_people.works: "Acadiensis II" (1971); "'Limited Identities' and Canadian Historical Scholarship" (1988); "'Limited Identities' Revisited" (2000)

representative_people.name: T. W. Acheson
representative_people.context: Traced Maritime industrial growth under the National Policy tariff and its subordination to Montreal capital in the 1890s (1972, opening read).
representative_people.works: "The National Policy and the Industrialization of the Maritimes, 1880–1910" (1972)

representative_people.name: Ernest R. Forbes
representative_people.context: Historian of Maritime regional protest (1979) and of the region's stereotypes (1989); his article opened the first issue of Acadiensis (1971).
representative_people.works: The Maritime Rights Movement (1979); Challenging the Regional Stereotype (1989)

representative_people.name: Gerald Friesen
representative_people.context: Author of the standard prairie synthesis (1984); in 2000 a prairie historian's reading of the "Acadiensis generation", and a national framework linking Innis to social history.
representative_people.works: The Canadian Prairies (1984); "Atlantic Canada's Historical Writing Today" (2000); Citizens and Nation (2000)

representative_people.name: Doug Owram
representative_people.context: Studied the central-Canadian expansionist movement and its idea of the West (1980, description). Primary placement proposed in cdn_intellectual_cultural.

representative_people.name: Sarah Carter
representative_people.context: Prairie reserve agriculture and government policy (1990); catalogue level here. Primary placement proposed in native_newcomer; also in the settler-colonialism draft.

representative_people.name: Bill Waiser
representative_people.context: Provincial synthesis of Saskatchewan (2005) and, with Blair Stonechild, a history of First Nations and 1885 (1997).
representative_people.works: Saskatchewan: A New History (2005); Loyal till Death (1997, with Stonechild)

representative_people.name: Jean Barman
representative_people.context: British Columbia synthesis (1991) building on Ormsby and on new research, with attention to contemporaries' voices (BC Studies review).
representative_people.works: The West Beyond the West (1991; 3rd ed. 2007)

representative_people.name: Cole Harris
representative_people.context: Historical geographer of colonialism and geographical change in British Columbia (existing atlas source). Primary placement proposed in settler_colonialism (groups.json); also listed for the existing environment entry.

representative_people.name: Margaret Conrad
representative_people.context: Co-author with James Hiller of the Atlantic synthesis (2001; 2nd ed. 2010, introduction "A region in the making").

representative_people.name: John G. Reid
representative_people.context: Atlantic historian of Acadia and Mi'kma'ki; lead author of a collaborative volume on 1710 from imperial, colonial, Acadian and Indigenous perspectives (2004) and an early analyst of fragmentation in general syntheses (1987).
representative_people.works: The "Conquest" of Acadia, 1710 (2004, with Basque et al.); "Towards the Elusive Synthesis" (1987)

representative_people.name: Maurice Basque
representative_people.context: Acadian historian, co-author of the 2004 volume on the "Conquest" of Acadia; co-authorship only is verified here.

representative_people.name: R. W. (Ruth) Sandwell
representative_people.context: Rural history of Saltspring Island (2005), which Perry's review says shows "that big ideas can help us understand small places". Also listed for the environment entry.

representative_people.name: Robert Painchaud
representative_people.context: Francophone historian of the Church and French settlement in the Prairie West, 1870–1915; he died in 1978 and the book appeared posthumously in 1987 (RHAF review), so its scholarship belongs to the 1970s.
representative_people.works: Un rêve français dans le peuplement de la Prairie (1987)

representative_people.name: Fernand Harvey
representative_people.context: Compares the construction of regional identity in the West, the Maritimes and Quebec, where regional studies chose the intraprovincial rather than the interprovincial scale (2006, abstract).
representative_people.works: "Identity and Scales of Regionalism in Canada and Quebec" (2006)

representative_people.name: Gerald M. Craig
representative_people.context: Wrote the Upper Canada volume of the Canadian Centenary Series (1963), the standard provincial synthesis for the period 1784–1841 (catalogue level).

representative_people.name: H. V. Nelles
representative_people.context: Studied the Ontario government and the development of forests, mines and hydro-electric power, 1849–1941 (title and chapter level). Also on the cdn_intellectual_cultural roster.

representative_people.name: Ian M. Drummond
representative_people.context: Economic history of Ontario from Confederation to the Second World War, in the Ontario Historical Studies Series (catalogue level). Primary placement proposed in cdn_political_national.

representative_people.name: Douglas McCalla
representative_people.context: Economic history of Upper Canada, 1784–1870 (catalogue level).

representative_people.name: N. E. S. (Naomi) Griffiths
representative_people.context: An authority on Acadia before the deportation of 1755 (RHAF review); traced the emergence of Acadian identity (2005) and the contexts of Acadian history to 1784 (1992).
representative_people.works: The Contexts of Acadian History, 1686–1784 (1992); From Migrant to Acadian (2005)

representative_people.name: Geoffrey Plank
representative_people.context: Studied the British campaign against the peoples of Acadia (2001; title level).

representative_people.name: John Mack Faragher
representative_people.context: An American historian whose narrative of the expulsion of the Acadians (2005) is the most-cited Acadian work in the 2009–2026 PhD corpus (10 PhDs; title level).

representative_people.name: Ian McKay
representative_people.context: Asked in 2000 whether "region" can hold the 1990s histories of gender, ethnicity and community, which put "a question mark over the very concept of an 'Atlantic Canada'" (pp. 89–90). Primary placement proposed in liberal_order_framework.
representative_people.works: "A Note on 'Region' in Writing the History of Atlantic Canada" (2000)

strands.title: Limited identities
strands.focus: Cook's phrase (1967) and Careless's programme (1969); Buckner (2000) explains the different motives of Cook and Careless (Quebec and national unity) and of Atlantic historians.
strands.works: Ramsay Cook, "Canadian Centennial Cerebrations," International Journal 22, no. 4 (1967): 659–663.; J. M. S. Careless, "'Limited Identities' in Canada," Canadian Historical Review 50, no. 1 (1969): 1–10.; Phillip A. Buckner, "'Limited Identities' and Canadian Historical Scholarship: An Atlantic Provinces Perspective," Journal of Canadian Studies 23, no. 1–2 (1988): 177–198.; P. A. Buckner, "'Limited Identities' Revisited: Regionalism and Nationalism in Canadian History," Acadiensis 30, no. 1 (Autumn 2000): 4–15.

strands.title: The Prairie West
strands.focus: Provincial and regional syntheses (Morton 1957, Friesen 1984, Waiser 2005), the expansionist idea of the West (Owram 1980), reserve policy and 1885 (Carter 1990; Stonechild and Waiser 1997), and the Church and francophone settlement (Painchaud, a 1970s study published posthumously in 1987).
strands.works: W. L. Morton, Manitoba: A History (Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 1957; 2nd ed. 1967).; Gerald Friesen, The Canadian Prairies: A History (Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 1984).; Bill Waiser, Saskatchewan: A New History (Calgary: Fifth House, 2005).; Doug Owram, Promise of Eden: The Canadian Expansionist Movement and the Idea of the West, 1856–1900 (Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 1980).; Sarah Carter, Lost Harvests: Prairie Indian Reserve Farmers and Government Policy (Montreal and Kingston: McGill-Queen's University Press, 1990).; Blair Stonechild and Bill Waiser, Loyal till Death: Indians and the North-West Rebellion (Calgary: Fifth House, 1997).; Robert Painchaud, Un rêve français dans le peuplement de la Prairie (Saint-Boniface: Éditions des Plaines, 1987).

strands.title: Atlantic Canada and Acadiensis
strands.focus: Acadiensis (1971) as a regional programme; deindustrialization and the National Policy (Acheson 1972); regional protest (Forbes 1979); Atlantic synthesis (Conrad and Hiller 2001). Acadia has its own strand below.
strands.works: P. A. Buckner, "Acadiensis II," Acadiensis 1, no. 1 (Autumn 1971): 3ff.; T. W. Acheson, "The National Policy and the Industrialization of the Maritimes, 1880–1910," Acadiensis 1, no. 2 (Spring 1972): 3–28.; Ernest R. Forbes, The Maritime Rights Movement, 1919–1927: A Study in Canadian Regionalism (Montreal: McGill-Queen's University Press, 1979).; Ernest R. Forbes, Challenging the Regional Stereotype: Essays on the 20th Century Maritimes (Fredericton: Acadiensis Press, 1989).; Margaret R. Conrad and James K. Hiller, Atlantic Canada (Don Mills: Oxford University Press, 2001); 2nd ed., Atlantic Canada: A History (2010).

strands.title: Acadia (Atlantic)
strands.focus: Acadia before and after the expulsion of 1755. In the PhD corpus this is a substantial and rising literature: 101 of 1,303 PhDs (2009–2026) cite Acadian history works, 5.1% in 2009–14 and 8.9% in 2020–26, 23 of them at francophone universities. Griffiths, an authority on pre-1755 Acadia, wrote on its contexts to 1784 (1992) and the emergence of Acadian identity (2005); Plank (2001) and Faragher (2005) studied the British campaign against the peoples of Acadia and the expulsion; Reid, Basque and colleagues read the 1710 conquest from imperial, Acadian and Mi'kmaw perspectives (2004). Landry and Lang's Histoire de l'Acadie (2001) is a francophone university synthesis of Maritime Acadia over four centuries that sets out to recount the experience of the whole Acadian people, not only its elite. Most of these works are post-2000 (partial extension). Readers of this literature also engage Quebec historiography (lift 3.2): see the comparison with quebec_historiography.
strands.works: N. E. S. Griffiths, The Contexts of Acadian History, 1686–1784 (Montreal and Kingston: McGill-Queen's University Press, 1992).; Geoffrey Plank, An Unsettled Conquest: The British Campaign against the Peoples of Acadia (Philadelphia: University of Pennsylvania Press, 2001).; Nicolas Landry and Nicole Lang, Histoire de l'Acadie (Sillery: Septentrion, 2001).; John G. Reid, Maurice Basque, Elizabeth Mancke, Barry Moody, Geoffrey Plank and William Wicken, The "Conquest" of Acadia, 1710: Imperial, Colonial, and Aboriginal Constructions (Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 2004).; N. E. S. Griffiths, From Migrant to Acadian: A North American Border People, 1604–1755 (Montreal and Kingston: McGill-Queen's University Press, 2005).; John Mack Faragher, A Great and Noble Scheme: The Tragic Story of the Expulsion of the French Acadians from Their American Homeland (New York: W. W. Norton, 2005).

strands.title: British Columbia
strands.focus: From Ormsby's centennial history (1958) to Barman's synthesis (1991), Harris's colonial geography (1997) and Sandwell's rural history (2005). Reimer's history of BC historical writing (2009) ends in 1958 with Ormsby and Lamb's first generation of BC historians.
strands.works: Margaret A. Ormsby, British Columbia: A History (Toronto: Macmillan, 1958).; Jean Barman, The West Beyond the West: A History of British Columbia (Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 1991; rev. ed. 1996; 3rd ed. 2007).; R. W. Sandwell, Contesting Rural Space: Land Policy and Practices of Resettlement on Saltspring Island, 1859–1891 (Montreal and Kingston: McGill-Queen's University Press, 2005).; Chad Reimer, Writing British Columbia History, 1784–1958 (Vancouver: UBC Press, 2009).

strands.title: Ontario and Upper Canada
strands.focus: Provincial history of Ontario: Craig's Upper Canada volume in the Canadian Centenary Series (1963); Nelles on the provincial state and the development of forests, mines and hydro-electric power (1974); economic histories of the province (Drummond 1987, Ontario Historical Studies Series) and of Upper Canada (McCalla 1993); Baskerville's concise history (2005) as a later synthesis. Ontario is the province most often named in 2009–2026 History PhD titles (78 of 1,303 match 'Ontario' or 'Toronto'; 6.6% in 2009–14, 3.7% in 2020–26). Works were chosen by PhD citation counts (Nelles 34, McCalla 26, Craig 17, Drummond 15, Baskerville 12) and checked against catalogue and DOI records; no checked source frames Ontario within the limited-identities debate.
strands.works: Gerald M. Craig, Upper Canada: The Formative Years, 1784–1841 (Toronto: McClelland and Stewart, 1963).; H. V. Nelles, The Politics of Development: Forests, Mines and Hydro-Electric Power in Ontario, 1849–1941 (Toronto: Macmillan of Canada, 1974; 2nd ed. 2005).; Ian M. Drummond, Progress without Planning: The Economic History of Ontario from Confederation to the Second World War (Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 1987).; Douglas McCalla, Planting the Province: The Economic History of Upper Canada, 1784–1870 (Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 1993).; Peter A. Baskerville, Sites of Power: A Concise History of Ontario (Oxford University Press, 2005).
strands.north_and_newfoundland_note: The North and Newfoundland and Labrador are small in the PhD corpus (about 18 and 9 of 1,303 titles, 2009–2026) and get no strand; no checked source here covers their regional historiography.

strands.title: Quebec's regions and scales
strands.focus: Quebec regional history works at the intraprovincial scale (Harvey 2006); Histoire de la Gaspésie (1981) is one example. Distinct from interprovincial regionalism in the West and the Maritimes.
strands.works: Fernand Harvey, "Identity and Scales of Regionalism in Canada and Quebec: A Historical Approach," Norteamérica 1, no. 2 (2006): 77–96.; Jules Bélanger et al., Histoire de la Gaspésie (Montréal: Boréal Express; Institut québécois de recherche sur la culture, 1981); new ed. by Marc Desjardins et al. (Québec: Éditions de l'IQRC, 1999).

strands.title: Questioning region
strands.focus: McKay (2000) asks whether region survives the multiplication of subject positions; Friesen (2000) weighs lives against the abstraction of region; Buckner (2000) revisits limited identities.
strands.works: Ian McKay, "A Note on 'Region' in Writing the History of Atlantic Canada," Acadiensis 29, no. 2 (Spring 2000): 89–101.; Gerald Friesen, "Atlantic Canada's Historical Writing Today: No Howe?" Acadiensis 30, no. 1 (Autumn 2000): 64–72.; P. A. Buckner, "'Limited Identities' Revisited: Regionalism and Nationalism in Canadian History," Acadiensis 30, no. 1 (Autumn 2000): 4–15.

uptake.note: Steady: 14.4% (2009–14), 15.4% (2015–19), 14.8% (2020–26), the only one of these four drafts not falling. Most-cited works here: Friesen, Canadian Prairies (48 PhDs); Carter, Lost Harvests (47); Owram, Promise of Eden (43); Barman (27); Waiser (23); Harris 1997 (22). The steadiness comes mainly from Carter, Harris and Barman, whose primary placements lie elsewhere.

proposed_relationships.relationship: Regional history against the national themes
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: Buckner (1971, p. 3): historians "are still obsessed with the great 'national' themes", the CHR "has done very little to encourage local and regional history", and only the Atlantic Provinces lack a journal; footnote 1 cites Careless 1969. Buckner (2000, pp. 4–5) explains limited identities as a turn away from the nation-state frame. Targets the national frame, not every national historian. PhD context: 95 of 194 2009–2026 PhDs engaged with cdn_regional also engage the cdn_national_tradition anchor set (49% vs 13% of all; lift 3.69). Bibliographies record consultation, not influence.

McKay (2000, pp. 89–90) contrasts the 1990s agenda of gender, ethnicity and community with "1970s and early-1980s topics" of regional underdevelopment and class conflict, and calls the new pluralism "a continuation of … the social-history revolution of the 1960s and 1970s". Comparison: overlapping projects, not a hierarchy.

Harris's colonial geography of British Columbia (existing source: displacement and colonial geographical change) and Harvey (2006, abstract) on how geographic scale shapes regional identity in the West, the Maritimes and Quebec. Comparison; the settler-colonialism draft proposes its own Harris edge.

Harvey (2006, abstract): Quebec's regional studies, by historians and sociologists, chose the intraprovincial scale rather than the interprovincial one that structures the West and the Maritimes. Histoire de la Gaspésie (1981) is an example. Comparison. PhD context: 69 of 194 2009–2026 PhDs engaged with cdn_regional also engage the quebec_historiography anchor set (36% vs 16% of all; lift 2.27). Bibliographies record consultation, not influence. Acadia (added 2026-10-12, answers Q87): readers of Acadian history works (101 of 1,303 PhDs, 2009–2026) engage the quebec_historiography anchors at 50.5% (lift 3.23), more than any other group (answers/data-answers.json, Q86_87_acadia). Landry and Lang's francophone synthesis (2001) was reviewed in the RHAF; Griffiths's From Migrant to Acadian (2005) was reviewed there too. Comparison, not derivation: Acadian historiography is placed in cdn_regional (Atlantic), not in quebec_historiography.

Reid, Basque et al. (2004, abstract) treat 1710 through its effects on "aboriginal inhabitants, Acadians, and New Englanders" at local, regional and imperial scales; Carter (1990) and Stonechild and Waiser (1997) are western examples (catalogue level). The PhD overlap is the strongest of this entry's Canadian links. PhD context: 153 of 194 2009–2026 PhDs engaged with cdn_regional also engage the native_newcomer anchor set (79% vs 19% of all; lift 4.21). Bibliographies record consultation, not influence.

proposed_relationships.relationship: Regional economic history of the Maritimes
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: Acheson (1972, pp. 3–4) revisits the National Policy from the Maritimes: a staple economy, rapid industrial growth under the tariff in the 1880s, then local entrepreneurs' acquiescence "to the industrial leadership of the Montreal business community". A specific regional contribution; no general claim about economic history.

relationships_considered_not_proposed.reason: The highest PhD overlap (122 PhDs, lift 5.09) comes from Carter and Harris, who anchor both. The settler-colonialism draft already proposes Harris edges; no checked source here frames regional history as settler-colonial. Leave to that draft.
Sandwell and Harris are placed in the environment entry; rural history overlaps, but no checked source here states the link.
McKay and Acheson touch class and deindustrialization in the Maritimes; no checked text links regional and working-class history directly.

open_questions: Harris and Carter are anchors here but primarily placed elsewhere (settler_colonialism; native_newcomer). Keep them as secondary roster members?
Should Ontario, the North and Newfoundland have a strand? No checked source here covers them.
Is Quebec's intraprovincial regional history (Harvey; Histoire de la Gaspésie) best shown here as a contrast, or only in quebec_historiography?

Acadian historiography: Basque is here only as a co-author. Should a francophone Acadian historian be added (to be verified), or does Acadia belong in quebec_historiography or a separate Atlantic strand?
Painchaud's date (1986 or 1987) is unresolved in Open Library; 1987 is used, following the citation graph.
Margaret Ormsby has no candidates.csv row (3 PhDs, 2009–2026, for her 1958 book). Keep her as an early regional historian and one of few women in these rosters?

question_resolutions.summary: Harris and Carter kept as secondary roster rows (their readers engage regional history at lifts 4.7 and 4.4).

Added an Ontario strand (Craig 1963, Nelles 1974, Drummond 1987, McCalla 1993; Baskerville 2005 as extension), chosen by 2009–2026 PhD citation counts and checked against catalogue and DOI records, with roster rows for Craig, Nelles, Drummond and McCalla. A note covers the North (about 18 titles) and Newfoundland (9), which get no strand.
No change to this entry: Quebec's intraprovincial regional history stays a contrast strand here; its fuller treatment belongs to quebec_historiography.
